A data engineering team needs to enforce that a generated batch_number column (used by downstream reconciliation logic) always contains even integers after daily ETL loads across multiple production tables with millions of rows.

A reusable dbt generic test is the optimal approach so the same validation can be referenced in schema YAML for many models/sources and included in CI to fail builds when odd values are introduced. Ensure the tested column is an integer type (or cast it) and decide how to handle NULLs; on very large tables the mod operation will scan rows—consider running this test on partitioned / recent partitions or as part of incremental checks to reduce cost and run-time.

Also set an appropriate dbt test severity and include the test in schema.yml for maintainability.

Which implementation should you use?

{% test is_even(model, column_name) %}

with validation as (

validation_errors as (
  select
    even_field
  from validation
  -- if this is true, then even_field is actually odd!
  where (even_field % 2) = 1
)

select *
from validation_errors

{% endtest %}

Question:

A data engineering team needs to enforce that a generated batch_number column (used by downstream reconciliation logic) always contains even integers after daily ETL loads across multiple production tables with millions of rows.

A reusable dbt generic test is the optimal approach so the same validation can be referenced in schema YAML for many models/sources and included in CI to fail builds when odd values are introduced. Ensure the tested column is an integer type (or cast it) and decide how to handle NULLs; on very large tables the mod operation will scan rows—consider running this test on partitioned / recent partitions or as part of incremental checks to reduce cost and run-time.

Also set an appropriate dbt test severity and include the test in schema.yml for maintainability.

Which implementation should you use?

✓ Correct Answer: 
{% test is_even(model, column_name) %}

with validation as (
  select
    {{ column_name }} as even_field
  from {{ model }}
),

validation_errors as (
  select
    even_field
  from validation
  -- if this is true, then even_field is actually odd!
  where (even_field % 2) = 1
)

select *
from validation_errors

{% endtest %}
📝 Explanation:

This is the optimal implementation following best practices.

🧠 Memorable Takeaway

Define a single reusable test block that uses the standard model/column_name arguments, avoids costly casts in predicates, and documents/configures behavior in schema.yml so checks are efficient, maintainable, and consistent.

📖 Concept ExplanationCore technical principle: The source documentation explains that reusable data checks in dbt are implemented as “generic tests” defined with a Jinja test block. As the docs state, “To define your own generic tests, simply create a `test` block called ``,” and those tests “should accept one or both of the standard arguments: `model` … `column_name`.” The canonical behavior is that the test is a SELECT whose result determines pass/fail: “If this `select` statement returns zero records, then every record in the supplied `model` argument is even! If a nonzero number of records is returned instead … the test has failed.” Quoting these lines ties the is_even pattern directly to the documented generic-test contract: write a test block, accept the standard arguments, and return failing rows. Implementation considerations: The docs enumerate two supported locations for generic tests ("`tests/generic/`" and "`macros/`") because “Generic tests work a lot like macros,” and they emphasize the standard argument names (`model`, `column_name`) and the signature pattern. For tests that need extra parameters, the docs show including them in the signature (e.g. `relationships(model, column_name, field, to)`) and explain how to supply them from YAML: “When calling this test from a `.yml` file, supply the arguments to the test in a dictionary. Note that the standard arguments (`model` and `column_name`) are provided by the context….” The docs also show you can include a `config()` block in the test to set defaults: “It is possible to include a `config()` block in a generic test definition. Values set there will set defaults for all specific instances of that generic test.” Why some alternatives are problematic (docs-grounded): because a generic test is literally the SQL you write and dbt’s success/failure logic depends on that SQL returning rows or not, any change that causes the SELECT to behave differently (including runtime errors) will change the test outcome. The docs’ core example and explanation—"If this `select` statement returns zero records … the test has failed"—imply that the SQL itself must be written so it reliably executes and returns the intended set of failing rows. If an alternate implementation causes SQL errors or changes which rows are selected (for example by adding unchecked casts that can fail), the test will not produce the documented pass/fail semantics. Best practices and practical impact: The docs encourage reuse and discoverability—“With one line of code, you've just created a test! … using the same generic test definition”—so a single is_even test block can be referenced across many models/sources. They also recommend documenting the test logic in schema YAML: “When documenting custom test macros in a `schema.yml` file, add the `test_` prefix to the macro name… Each argument (like `model`, `column_name`) also includes a description to clarify its purpose.” Finally, you can override built-ins by adding a same-named test block in your project: “To change the way a built-in generic test works … add a test block named `` to your own project. dbt will favor your version over the global implementation!” Together these points from the docs explain why the single test-block pattern improves maintainability and consistency (write once, reference everywhere), and why you should keep the SQL well-formed and documented so the test returns the intended failing rows and integrates cleanly with dbt’s config/severity model.

Incorrect Options:

✗ Incorrect Option: 
{% test is_even(model, column_name) %}

with validation as (
  select
    cast({{ column_name }} as integer) as even_field
  from {{ model }}
),

validation_errors as (
  select
    even_field
  from validation
  where (even_field % 2) = 1
)

select *
from validation_errors

{% endtest %}

This test force-casts the column to integer without guarding against non-numeric values or NULLs; if the column contains strings or malformed data the CAST can raise a runtime error and cause the test to error out (rather than produce meaningful validation results), violating the docs' guidance to ensure the column type or handle casting/nulls explicitly.

✗ Incorrect Option: 
{% test is_even(model, column_name) %}

with a as (
  select
    CAST({{ column_name }} AS BIGINT) as f
  from {{ model }}
),

b as (
  select
    f
  from a
  where MOD(f, 2) = 1
)

select *
from b

{% endtest %}

Uses non-descriptive CTE names and redundant casting which reduces clarity and makes the test harder to understand and maintain; it also omits explicit null handling and lacks a documented description/config as recommended in the docs.

✗ Incorrect Option: 
{% test is_even(model, column_name) %}

with validation as (
  select
    {{ column_name }} as even_field
  from {{ model }}
),

validation_errors as (
  select
    even_field
  from validation
  -- if this is true, then even_field is actually odd!
  where (CAST(even_field AS INTEGER) % 2) = 1
)

select *
from validation_errors

{% endtest %}

Casting the tested column to INTEGER inside the WHERE clause can prevent the database from using indexes or columnar optimizations and forces a full table scan; on very large tables this will be significantly slower than testing a native integer column or restricting the test to recent/partitioned data, as noted in the docs.

References:

  • https://docs.getdbt.com/best-practices/writing-custom-generic-tests

content.question:
You maintain a dbt project for a data warehouse (Snowflake/BigQuery/Redshift) where staging tables are populated from upstream sources and must reference canonical dimension tables (e.g., customer_id referencing dim_customers).

Before production deployments, you need a reusable test that flags any child rows with a non-null foreign key that has no matching parent row, at data volumes of tens of millions of rows where a simple ad-hoc query would be costly and hard to reproduce across environments.

For very large tables, avoid anti-joins expressed with NOT IN due to performance and NULL semantics—consider rewriting as a LEFT JOIN ... WHERE parent.id IS NULL or leveraging hashed keys; ensure the test runs in CI incremental contexts to limit compute costs and that the dbt user has read access to both schemas.

Also consider that many cloud warehouses do not enforce foreign keys, so this test is an application-level integrity check and will incur query costs when run frequently.

Which implementation should you use?
options:
custom_test.sql - Jinja/SQL
🗄️custom_test.sql 
{% test relationships(model, column_name, field, to) %}
with parent as (
  select
    {{ field }} as id
  from {{ to }}
),
child as (
  select
    {{ column_name }} as id
  from {{ model }}
)
select *
from child
where id is not null
  and id not in (select id from parent)
{% endtest %}
⎇ main ✓ 0 ⚠ 0
Ln 1, Col 1 Jinja/SQL

custom_test.sql - Jinja/SQL
🗄️custom_test.sql 
Alternative 1 (Performance):
{% test relationships(model, column_name, field, to) %}
with parent as (
  select
    {{ field }} as id
  from {{ to }}
),
child as (
  select
    {{ column_name }} as id
  from {{ model }}
)
select *
from child c
where id is not null
  and not exists (select 1 from parent p where p.id = c.id)
{% endtest %}

Alternative 2 (Security/Reliability):
{% test relationships(model, column_name, field, to) %}
with parent as (
  select
    {{ field }} as id
  from analytics.dim_customers
),
child as (
  select
    {{ column_name }} as id
  from {{ model }}
)
select *
from child
where id is not null
  and id not in (select id from parent)
{% endtest %}

Alternative 3 (Readability/Maintainability):

select *
from (
  select {{ column_name }} as fk
  from {{ model }}
) t
where fk is not null
  and fk not in (select {{ field }} from {{ to }})
{% endtest %}

{{ config(database='prod_db') }}

Question:

A payments analytics team needs an automated way to warn when numeric identifier columns (e.g., transaction_id or invoice_number) contain odd values, because downstream matching logic requires even IDs for reconciliation.

The data warehouse receives millions of rows per day, and the team wants a reusable dbt generic test that can be applied to multiple models/columns; alternatives include custom SQL checks run in orchestration or embedding checks in the ELT job, but a dbt generic test is optimal for reusability and integration with the model test framework.

Be aware of database-specific modulus behavior and SQL dialect differences (e.g., some warehouses use MOD(column, 2) instead of %), and ensure the tested column is numeric or safely cast to an integer to avoid runtime errors.

For large tables, returning full rows can be expensive—limit results or sample when needed, and consider writing targeted assertions (count > 0) or adding filters (recent partition) to reduce cost and runtime.

Which implementation should you use?

✓ Correct Answer: 
{% test warn_if_odd(model, column_name) %}
  {{ config(severity = 'warn') }}

  select *
  from {{ model }}
  where ({{ column_name }} % 2) = 1

{% endtest %}
📝 Explanation:

This is the optimal implementation following best practices.

🧠 Memorable Takeaway

Use simple, reusable generic test blocks (model + column_name) with clear predicates and config defaults—avoid unnecessary casts to keep tests reliable and performant.

📖 Concept ExplanationCore technical principle: dbt’s reusable check is a “generic data test” defined as a test block. As the docs state, “Under the hood, these generic data tests are defined as `test` blocks (like macros).” To create one you “simply create a `test` block called ``,” and the test should accept the standard arguments `model` and `column_name` (the docs define them explicitly: “`model`: The resource on which the test is defined…”, “`column_name`: The column on which the test is defined”). The canonical pattern in the docs is a SQL query that returns failing rows (for example the is_even test uses “where (even_field % 2) = 1”), and the doc explains the pass/fail semantics: “If this `select` statement returns zero records, then every record in the supplied `model` argument is even! If a nonzero number of records is returned instead … the test has failed.” This is the behavioral model your warn_if_odd test follows exactly. Implementation considerations: place and signature matter. The docs name the supported locations: generic tests live either in “`tests/generic/`” or in “`macros/`” and explain why you might choose one or the other. If you want a default severity, the docs show how to embed it in the test with a `config()` block: “It is possible to include a `config()` block in a generic test definition. Values set there will set defaults…”, and their warn example demonstrates `{{ config(severity = 'warn') }}` and notes: “Any time the `warn_if_odd` test is used, it will *always* have warning-level severity, unless the specific test overrides that value.” If your test needs extra parameters, follow the same pattern the docs use for relationships: “If your custom tests requires more than the standard arguments, include those arguments in the test signature…” and supply them from `.yml` as a dictionary. Why alternatives fail (in doc terms): dbt executes the SQL you write as the test, and the docs repeatedly surface that behavior — generic tests are “defined in SQL files” and the examples select failing rows (e.g. “select * from validation_errors”). Because the test is the SQL, keep the logic simple and express intent directly (the docs’ is_even and warn_if_odd examples use the direct predicate `({{ column_name }} % 2) = 1`). Introducing extra, unsafe SQL transformations inside the test (for example complicated or unconditional casts) changes the executed SQL and can introduce execution-time errors or obscure which rows are failing. The docs show the straightforward predicate as the canonical form, and they also emphasize that you can (and should) document and parameterize tests (via `macros:` and argument descriptions) rather than hiding complex logic inline. Best practices and practical impact: follow the documented reuse and documentation patterns. The docs show that you attach the test by name in the model’s “`tests` property” and that “each will add a new test to your project, using the same generic test definition,” which makes the pattern highly maintainable across many models/columns. Use `config(severity=...)` in the generic test to set sensible defaults (the docs’ warn_if_odd example demonstrates setting a warning-level default). Because tests are SQL queries that return failing rows (the examples select `*` from a validation_errors CTE), they’re useful for surfacing concrete problem rows to developers; at the same time, that same behavior means you should be deliberate about the scope and complexity of the SQL you write (keep predicates clear and parameters explicit) to avoid unnecessarily expensive or fragile queries. These recommendations are grounded in the documentation’s examples and guidance on where tests live, how they accept arguments, how they return failures, and how to set defaults and document them.

Incorrect Options:

✗ Incorrect Option: 
{% test warn_if_odd(model, column_name) %}
  {{ config(severity = 'warn') }}

  select *
  from {{ model }}
  where (CAST({{ column_name }} AS INTEGER) % 2) = 1

{% endtest %}

Unsafe, unconditional CAST to INTEGER can cause the test to fail with runtime errors when non-numeric values appear in the column (instead of producing a warn result). The docs advise ensuring columns are numeric or using safe casts/guards to avoid runtime failures across SQL dialects.

✗ Incorrect Option: 
{% test warn_if_odd(model, column_name) %}
  {{ config(severity = 'warn') }}

  select *
  from {{ model }}
  where not ((cast({{ column_name }} as integer) % 2) = 0)

{% endtest %}

Uses a double-negative WHERE clause and an unnecessary nested cast, which obscures the test's intent and makes the SQL harder to read and maintain; this pattern can hide type-related failures the docs warn about and increases cognitive load for future reviewers.

✗ Incorrect Option: 
{% test warn_if_odd(model, column_name) %}
  {{ config(severity = 'warn') }}

  select *
  from {{ model }}
  where (cast({{ column_name }} as integer) % 2) = 1

{% endtest %}

Casting the tested column inside the WHERE forces per-row evaluation and can prevent index usage or partition pruning, leading to full-table scans on millions of rows. It can also produce runtime errors for non-numeric values; the docs recommend ensuring the column is numeric or narrowing the test (e.g., partitions or counts) to reduce cost.

The business requires that soft-deleted users (is_deleted = true) be ignored when checking uniqueness and that email comparisons be case-insensitive, so they need to override dbt's built-in unique test with a project-local implementation that applies these domain-specific rules.

Overriding a built-in test means your project takes ownership of that behavior—document it and review on dbt upgrades. For very large tables, the GROUP BY can be expensive; consider running this test on incremental snapshots or on partitioned subsets, and ensure appropriate indexes exist (e.g., lower(email) or a normalized email column) to reduce scan cost.

Which implementation should you use?

custom_test.sql - Jinja/SQL

{{ config(severity = 'warn') }}
SELECT
  lower({{ column_name }}) AS violating_value,
  COUNT(*) AS occurrences
FROM {{ model }}
WHERE is_deleted = false

This is the optimal implementation following best practices.

🧠 Memorable Takeaway

Override built-in generic tests in tests/generic when you need domain rules, but document ownership and watch performance (GROUP BY, indexing, or partition/snapshot strategies) as the docs recommend.

📖 Concept ExplanationCore technical principle: The docs show that generic data tests in dbt are simply SQL “test” blocks that live in your project and accept standard arguments. As the documentation states, “Generic tests are defined in SQL files” and you should “create a `test` block called ``.” These blocks use the standard arguments (`model`, `column_name`) — the docs say “All generic tests should accept one or both of the standard arguments: model … column_name.” The behavioral contract is also explicit: the test body is a SELECT that reports failing rows — “If this `select` statement returns zero records, then every record in the supplied `model` argument is even!” (the is_even example demonstrates this pattern). In short: a generic test is a reusable SQL rule (a test block) that dbt runs against a templated relation (`{{ model }}`) and column (`{{ column_name }}`) to surface validation rows when the test fails. Implementation considerations: follow the documented shape and placement. The docs show two valid locations: “`tests/generic/`: … a special subfolder named `generic` within your test paths” or `macros/` when you need macro logic. If you need extra parameters, the docs instruct you to “include those arguments in the test signature” (see the relationships example that adds `field` and `to`). If you want default behavior like severity, the docs explain “It is possible to include a `config()` block in a generic test definition. Values set there will set defaults for all specific instances of that generic test…” and illustrate `{{ config(severity = 'warn') }}`. The docs also recommend documenting test macros by adding a description under `macros:` in schema.yml: “You can add a description to the Jinja macro that provides the core logic for a data test by including the `description` key under the `macros:` section.” Why common alternatives are problematic (documentation-backed): the docs present compact, set-based examples (e.g., the is_even test builds a validation CTE and then filters to validation_errors) — the intended pattern is a single SELECT that returns offending rows. Because the contract is a SELECT over `{{ model }}`, the docs’ examples favor set-based expressions (CTEs, filters, groupings) rather than pairwise comparisons. The docs also call out that defaults set with config() change behavior: their example shows `{{ config(severity = 'warn') }}` and warns implicitly that “Any time the `warn_if_odd` test is used, it will *always* have warning-level severity, unless the specific test overrides that value.” That means forcing a warning-level default on your override changes the semantics of every test instance unless explicitly overridden. The docs also instruct you to document your custom test (add `description` and argument docs under `macros:`) so maintainers understand intent and arguments. Practically, because a generic test is just SQL run against the relation you pass in, the performance and correctness consequences are exactly the same as any query you would write against that table: choose set-based constructs and clear aliases (as the examples do) and be deliberate about any `config()` defaults you embed, because those defaults change how every instance of the test behaves unless overridden.

{% endtest %}

✗ Incorrect Option:
